insights.statement: ARR growth fell from 25% to 9.2% because net new ARR fell by €5.6M (€10.4M to €4.8M): churned ARR rose by €4.5M (€3.3M to €7.8M) and expansion fell by €1.3M, while new ARR rose by €0.2M (€9.4M to €9.6M).
insights.decision_relevance: The slowdown is a retention and expansion problem; the CRO's proposal addresses new sales, which did not fall.

insights.statement: The sales engine did not weaken: pipeline created rose from €38.9M to €45.9M, the win rate held between 23% and 24% every quarter and deals won rose from 175 to 193; the slowdown did not come from new sales, so it cannot come from price competition in new deals.
insights.decision_relevance: Tests and rejects the diagnosis behind the 30-AE request.
insights.caveat: Price is still the stated reason for 34% of lost deals and pipeline grew faster than new ARR; competitive pressure exists at the margin but is not what changed between 2024 and 2025.

insights.statement: Churn is a first-year problem: customers onboarded in the previous 12 months churned 26% of ARR versus 9% for mature customers; they held 35% of opening ARR but 60.3% of churned ARR, and first-year churn rose 14 PP from 12% in 2024.
insights.decision_relevance: Points the 2026 budget at onboarding of new customers rather than at the installed base or at new sales.
insights.caveat: The 2024 first-year rate comes from CS notes and is assumed to be on the same ARR basis.

insights.statement: The onboarding cut is the most likely cause: the team went from 14 to 6 people in February 2025, median time to first value rose from 21 to 48 days, and 58% of the 64 churned customers interviewed never fully implemented the product versus 17% who moved to a competitor and 14% who cite price.
insights.decision_relevance: Identifies a reversible management decision as the root cause.
insights.caveat: Causality rests on timing and exit interviews; no controlled comparison exists.

insights.statement: The onboarding saving was a false economy: it saved €0.8M a year while first-year churn above the 2024 rate cost about €2.5M of ARR in 2025.
insights.decision_relevance: Restoring the team is the cheapest growth lever available, roughly three times its cost in ARR in year one.
insights.caveat: 2.5 EUR M is an upper bound for what reversing the cut recovers: it assumes first-year churn returns fully to 12%.

insights.statement: The CRO's €9M is the full-productivity run-rate of 30 AEs at €300k each; with a 9-month ramp, a Q1 hire delivers about €5.6M of new ARR in 2026, €3.4M short of the promise, for €3.6M a year.
insights.decision_relevance: The 2026 budget should not book 9 EUR M of AE-driven new ARR.
insights.caveat: 5.6 EUR M itself is an upper end: it assumes a linear ramp, all hires in place on 1 January and enough pipeline.

insights.statement: New customers won by extra AEs would enter an onboarding that loses 26% of first-year ARR, so hiring before fixing onboarding buys ARR that leaks within a year.
insights.decision_relevance: Sequencing: retention fix before, or at least alongside, sales capacity.

insights.statement: Expansion ARR fell by €1.3M (€4.3M to €3.0M); a link to poor implementation is plausible but untested, so the expansion lever is an upper bound.
insights.decision_relevance: Second retention lever; needs account-level validation before it is booked.
